Parchment
pärch´mĕnt
n. (prepared skin used as a writing material; the durable medium of the ancient books)
From Pergamum in Asia Minor, where the material was developed. The AV has it once, in the last letter Paul wrote: “the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Parchment is the durable writing material of the ancient world. Paul, near his execution, asks for three things: “The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments” (2Ti 4:13). Jeremiah's roll was cut and burned by a king, and rewritten: Jehoiakim “cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire” (Jer 36:23); “Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch… who wrote therein… all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire” (Jer 36:32). Job wished for permanence: “Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!” (Job 19:23). And John sees “a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals” (Rev 5:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines parchment as the skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing; and notes it was so called from Pergamus, where it is said to have been invented.

expand to see more

PARCHMENT, n. The skin of a sheep or goat dressed and prepared for writing.

The best parchments are from Pergamus, in Asia Minor, from which place they take their name.

VELLUM, n. A finer kind of parchment or skin, rendered clear and white for writing.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:13 — "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments."

Jer 36:23 — "And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth."

Jer 36:32 — "Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words."

Job 19:23 — "Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!"

Rev 5:1 — "And I saw in the right hand of him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals."

Modern Corruption

The Bible's physical transmission is treated as an embarrassment to its inspiration, and Scripture is entirely open about skins, scribes and burned rolls.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 36 is the chapter to give anyone worried that the Bible came to us through fragile human means, because it says so itself and draws the opposite conclusion. A prophet dictates; a scribe writes; the roll is read to a king; the king cuts it up with a penknife three or four leaves at a time and burns it; and the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah again, saying, Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words. Baruch writes it a second time, and there were added besides unto them many like words. The medium is destructible and the word is not.

Second Timothy 4:13 is the most human sentence in the New Testament and it belongs beside all this. Paul is in a Roman prison, expecting to die, and he asks for a cloak because it is cold, and for the books, but especially the parchments. Nobody knows what they were — his own copies of the Scriptures, most likely, perhaps notes or documents. What is certain is that a man at the end of a life like his still wanted to read, and thought the request worth putting in an inspired letter.

The doctrinal use is a caution against two errors. The first treats the text as though it descended without a history, and is then shaken by any manuscript question. The second treats the history as evidence against the doctrine. Scripture itself is unembarrassed: it names the scribes, records the burning, notes the second roll, and asks for the parchments. God's superintendence worked through skins and copyists and a prisoner's request, which is exactly the way He does everything else.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek membrana (G3200), parchment; biblion (G975), a book, scroll; Hebrew megillah (H4039), a roll; ta'ar hassopher (H8593), the scribe's penknife.

expand to see more

Greek membrana (G3200) — parchment; 2 Timothy 4:13 only.

Hebrew megillah (H4039) — roll, scroll; Jeremiah 36:2, 36:23, 36:28, 36:32, Ezekiel 2:9, Zechariah 5:1.

Greek biblion (G975) — book, scroll; Revelation 5:1–9, 2 Timothy 4:13, John 20:30.

Usage

"“The books, but especially the parchments” — asked for from a death cell."

"“Cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire” — and it was written again."

"“Oh that my words were now written!” — and they were."
